item.title: North Carolina peatland emits 130,000 tons of CO₂ yearly after 50 miles of ditches were cut
item.description: In a significant ecological effort, North Carolina is working to restore its ancient peatlands that suffered damage from farming practices impacting their carbon storage capabilities. The previous drainage systems caused water levels to drop, resulting in peat exposure to air and increased emissions. Restoration efforts include blocking these ditches to enhance land rehydration and restore the water table. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Unaccounted climate feedback loops may amplify warming by 20–30% this century, but cutting emissions will reduce risks
item.description: New research shows that warming-induced emissions—greenhouse gas emissions from natural sources driven by rising temperatures—could amplify global warming by approximately 20%–30% and add an estimated 0.2°C–0.4°C of warming this century on top of anthropogenic warming under different scenarios. These major additional drivers of warming are largely unaccounted for in current climate projections and policies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists say August was Earth's hottest month they've measured
item.description: Earth cooked to its hottest month on record in August, blowing far past a key climate threshold, due to the dangerous double whammy of human-caused climate change and a supersized El Niño, according to the European climate service Copernicus. Publicado también por: Phys.org. Fuente: NPR - World.

item.title: Climate ‘feedback loops’ could worsen global warming by 30%, study finds
item.description: Emissions of planet-heating methane and CO2 from natural sources are worsening the climate crisis, paper says Rising global temperatures caused by the burning of fossil fuels are transforming the world’s forests, wetlands and tundra to the point they are releasing emissions that could further worsen global heating by as much as 30%, a new study has found. As the world heats up, permafrost in the high latitudes is thawing, fiercer wildfires are burning in drying forests and wetlands and lakes are warming. All of these changes are themselves causing the release of planet-heating methane and… Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.description: Este 10 de septiembre se cumple un mes desde que un terremoto de magnitud 7,4 impactó a Colombia. Nuestro enviado especial, Maxime Pluvinet, estuvo en Pereira, una de las ciudades más afectadas, y nos contó cómo avanzan las labores de reconstrucción y cómo sobreviven, muchas sin un techo propio, las personas que lo perdieron todo. item.title: In 1987, Kansas brought bisons back to Konza Prairie; 29 yrs later, native plant richness rose 103%
item.description: In 1987, 30 bison were brought back to Kansas’ Konza Prairie as part of a long-term study of grassland ecology. Over the next 29 years, researchers found that bison grazing was linked to a major rise in native plant diversity. Native species richness increased by 103% locally and 86% across catchments, with the gains also recovering after a severe drought. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Why a wetter Tibetan Plateau still faces 'hot-dry' extremes: The roles of ENSO and the North Atlantic
item.description: Since the 1950s, the Tibetan Plateau has experienced pronounced warming and wetting. However, an overall shift toward wetter conditions does not necessarily mean that drought risk has diminished. On the contrary, against the backdrop of continued warming, compound hot-dry events—characterized by the simultaneous occurrence of high temperatures and drought—have become an increasingly important climate risk across the plateau. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Action on climate and air pollution likely to boost economy, UN says
item.description: Every US$1 invested in tackling climate change and air pollution together can generate around US$15 in economic benefits, according to a report published today by the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When disaster strikes, what happens to our pets?
item.description: As large-scale disasters—including earthquakes, torrential rains, typhoons and wildfires—become increasingly frequent, ensuring that pets as well as their owners can evacuate safely and receive appropriate care has become an important part of disaster preparedness. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Did wildfires help spark the invention of pottery?
item.description: A new study suggests that a period of intense fires and landscape upheaval in the ancient southern Levant may have helped create the conditions that led Neolithic communities to discover how fire could transform clay. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Costa Rica maps nearly 500 dominant tree species to protect forest biodiversity
item.description: Researchers mapped Costa Rica's diverse forest ecosystems by analyzing tree species composition. Satellite observations and environmental data helped create a national forest map. This map distinguishes forest types, including secondary forests, across varied landscapes. The findings highlight the importance of dominant tree species for understanding forest function. Better field inventories are still needed to improve future forest mapping efforts. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Portugal's Pinhal Interior shows why fire and floods are part of the same cycle
item.description: Across southern Europe, increasingly extreme heat, wildfire and intense rainfall are forcing planners to consider how one event can alter the risk of the next. Portugal's exceptionally wet winter and another summer of wildfire risk are an example of this. As a professor of architecture and climate change adaptation who has been following the cyclical nature of weather extremes in the Pinhal Interior region since the deadly 2017 fires, I explain why prevention must connect forests, settlements, slopes and waterways. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: California confirms rare sighting of gray wolf in Mendocino national forest
item.description: Officials say sighting a sign species – driven to extinction in state before reintroduction in 2011 – expanding its range A gray wolf has recently been seen in California’s Mendocino national forest for the first time since the species returned to the state 15 years ago, state wildlife officials confirmed. Officials in Lake county, which is about two hours north of San Francisco, said last week the California department of fish and wildlife (CDFW) had received reports of sightings in the forest in late August. The agency verified the presence of a wolf in the far north end of the county… Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: Optimizing tomato plant growth with microbes
item.description: Plants are home to a diverse array of microorganisms that support their growth and help them adapt to environmental stress—of which there has been an abundance lately. High temperatures and drought caused by human-induced climate change have led to reduced crop yields and the use of biofertilizers such as rhizosphere microorganisms, which help plants absorb nutrients and increase their resistance to disease and stress. Fuente: Phys.org.

By its end, some 4.5 million hectares (11.1 million acres) of the province's boreal forest had burned. item.title: Plants' response to rising CO₂ could put the brakes on dryland expansion
item.description: Drylands are defined as regions where rainfall is low relative to the atmosphere's ability to draw water from soil and plants. Expanding boundaries of these regions are frequent concerns in climate change considerations. While they can support large populations and ecosystems, dryland expansion can worsen water scarcity, land degradation and desertification. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 5.3-magnitude quake hits Tibet as region reels from deadly flash floods
item.description: A magnitude 5.3 earthquake struck Tibet recently, following another tremor last week. Devastating flash floods hit the Tibet-Nepal border on August 26, causing widespread destruction. The disaster has raised concerns over the fragile Qinghai-Tibet Plateau environment. Rising temperatures and glacier melt are cited as contributing factors to the floods. Nepal's death toll from the floods has risen to 1,357 people. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Heat waves inhibit antibiotic resistance in soils, but at a price
item.description: Extreme heat waves disrupt life in soil. Soil bacteria that produce and resist antibiotics switch into survival mode, temporarily reducing the number of resistance genes. At the same time, heat and drought are causing significant damage to soils and ecosystems, especially in cold, wet regions such as the Netherlands. This is evident from a large-scale European study by soil ecologist Franciska de Vries (University of Amsterdam) and colleagues. The findings are published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.
